Perps exploded in the last 2 years.

The top 10 perp DEXs processed $6.7T in trading volume in 2025 ($2.9T by Hyperliquid alone)

The next trillion-dollar opportunity is markets accessible beyond active traders.

@ensembleio is already testing this with leveraged strategy tokens, but its long-term upside is much bigger ↓

1. Strategies → Tokens

Ensemble recently launched on @HyperliquidX with three initial baskets:

→ BULL: Targets 3x long BTC + HYPE

→ BEAR: Targets 2x short BTC + ETH + SOL

→ VOL: Uses leveraged BTC shorts as a hedge, while keeping some funds in cash.

They also offer inverse versions, which take the opposite side of each strategy.

BEAR: 2x short exposure to BTC, ETH, and SOL

iBEAR: 2x long exposure to the same assets

Whichever strategy you choose, you don't have to open and manage those positions yourself.

Ensemble handles the trades and rebalancing behind the token.

2. Market-narrative Baskets

BULL, BEAR, and VOL are just the starting point. Ensemble is already exploring baskets built around popular crypto narratives, such as:

→ Bitcoin dominance
→ HYPE dominance
→ AI and memecoins
→ Real-world assets
→ The Hyperliquid ecosystem

Take AI, for example. You've got AI agents, decentralized computing projects, and plenty of other tokens competing under the same narrative.

In that sector, the basket's performance could depend heavily on which tokens they include.

The team also plans to use trader demand to decide which baskets come next, so it'll be fun to see what the community decides on.

3. Making Ensemble accessible beyond DeFi

@Ensembleio also plans to make its baskets easier to buy, as the roadmap includes two directions:

→ DEXs & CEXs: Allow users to buy baskets directly without minting them through Ensemble's vaults

→ Brokerages: Could bring these strategies to people outside DeFi

I think the second one could be particularly important.

There are plenty of people who bought $BTC or $ETH through Interactive Brokers or Charles Schwab but have never touched a perp trading terminal.

If they could access these baskets through platforms they already use, Ensemble could reach a much larger audience.

And with more people trading these baskets, Ensemble could build up the liquidity needed to support even more strategies.

4. ETF Scenario

Before ETFs became mainstream, getting diversified exposure to a sector meant buying and managing individual stocks yourself.

Now, if you're bullish on semiconductors, you can buy $SMH. If you want exposure to the S&P 500, you can buy $SPY.

One ticker gives you exposure to an entire investment thesis.

Imagine the same thing happening in crypto.

→ Bullish on AI? Buy an AI basket.

→ Expecting HYPE to outperform BTC? Buy a relative-performance basket.

→ Bearish on the crypto market? Buy a short basket.

The difference is that Ensemble could go beyond traditional ETFs by packaging actively managed, leveraged, and long/short strategies into single tokens.

Sure, it's different execution, but the underlying idea is similar – make complex market exposure accessible through one simple asset.

5. My Take

I've seen countless crypto narratives take over CT throughout the years, and I think turning those market opinions into tradable baskets has enormous potential.

As more markets become available on Hyperliquid, Ensemble could offer a growing range of strategies built around whatever the market is focused on.

In the longer term, I believe Ensemble could eventually do for crypto what ETFs did for stocks.

It would be fun to see Ensemble lead this category.

My reactions to You Can See Everything (as someone reasonably familiar with the case having read Bad Blood)  

— SPOILERS — 

- about an hour too long 
- Liz Holmes deserved a lesser sentence. The scale of the fraud was great yes but the harm done was minimal; her investors absorbed the loss. Retail wasn’t harmed and patients weren’t either. She was clearly the victim of a highly motivated and politicized prosecution. Frankly the investors completely failed in their diligence and deserved to lose their money 
- Liz is genuinely sympathetic. And a pathetic character. She clearly has surrendered all agency and is engaging in some kind of learned helplessness. Seems to bear no relation to the big corporate CEO she was before. Feel bad for her. There seems to be little upside to punishing her so severely. 
- didn’t remotely surprise me that she isn’t behind the X account. Did anyone think she was? How dumb do you have to be 
- Amanda Seyfriend was super unsympathetic and I ended up siding with the weird domineering boyfriend over her. Which takes some doing 
- the film was mostly an exercise in pointless navel gazing about the ethics of making a documentary; I can understand why a film student or a Hollywood obsessive might enjoy it but the stakes felt incredibly low. Shows the real disconnect between what Fielder and Seyfried think matters and what normal people do 
- Fielder was more interested in making meta jokes about Holmes/Seyfried than actually exploring Holmes’ psychology. The interesting parts of the films (the pre jail scenes) are too short 
- overall decent but wasn’t really about Liz at all it fell into the too familiar trap of the documentarian wondering about how much to insert himself into the story (gee that’s original) 
- I am flabbergasted that Fielder expected us to care about whether the subjects should be compensated. “It’s about the integrity of the documentary” uhh dude this is pretty low stakes stuff, also you’re comedian Nathan Fielder who makes a living getting people to beclown themselves, not Werner Herzog.

AI model competition is intensifying and the market structure is shifting faster than many expected.

Open-weight models are taking a growing share of token volume because they are good enough for a large range of workloads and meaningfully cheaper. At the same time, frontier closed models continue to lead on the highest-value tasks. The result is a more fragmented model layer, not a winner-take-most outcome.

From an investment perspective, this is constructive for the infrastructure layer. Lower effective pricing at the model layer tends to expand total usage rather than shrink it. More tokens, more agentic workflows and more enterprise customisation all translate into higher absolute demand for GPUs, high-bandwidth memory, networking, power and data-centre capacity - even as unit economics at the model providers compress.

The same dynamic is supportive for the application layer. When inference is cheaper and more widely available, the barrier to building specialised tools, agents and workflows drops. Value creation can shift further downstream into products and workflows that sit on top of multiple models.
